summary: At five people per square mile across 3,200 square miles of steep, forested terrain, Trinity County is roughly the size of Rhode Island and Delaware combined yet holds fewer residents than a single large apartment complex in downtown Los Angeles. This is the most sparsely populated county in California outside of Alpine, a place where the Trinity Alps — granite peaks topping 9,000 feet — feed the Trinity River through deep canyons blanketed in Douglas fir and ponderosa pine, and where the nearest freeway (Interstate 5) lies an hour's drive east over a mountain pass. The economy runs on timber, government services, and tourism; the U.S. Forest Service and county government are among the largest employers, and switching jobs without a long commute is genuinely difficult. A median home price of $329,000 against a median household income of roughly $53,500 yields a price-to-income ratio around 6.1 — not cheap by rural standards, especially given an 18% poverty rate that signals a thin local labor market. Summers are gorgeous, with average highs in the low sixties annually, nearly nine hours of daily sunshine, and direct access to wilderness trails from many front doors; winters bring real cold, with lows averaging around 40°F and mountain roads that can close in snow. Trinity is less a place you commute from and more a place you commit to — stunningly beautiful, profoundly remote, and structured around an economy where most paychecks come from public-sector or natural-resource work.
